outline.title: The Tutoring Puzzle
outline.summary: Open with the school report showing tutored students scored higher, invite visitors to guess why, then reveal that students who sought or were selected for tutoring may already have been stronger — so the score gap could be driven by what they brought in, not what tutoring added.
outline.rag_focus: observational versus interventional distributions; conditioning is not intervention
outline.anchor_use: Display the three-variable graph (PriorAchievement → TutoringAssignment, PriorAchievement → TestScore, TutoringAssignment → TestScore) and highlight the two paths from PriorAchievement to TestScore so visitors can see the hidden driver flowing alongside tutoring.
outline.target_misconception: If one group scores higher, the program must have caused the difference.
outline.interaction_hook: Ask visitors: 'Before we look at the graph, take a guess — why might tutored students score higher even if tutoring did nothing at all?' Collect two or three answers, then reveal the hidden PriorAchievement arrow.
outline.learning_arc_step: Start with a pattern people can recognize, then reveal the hidden driver.

outline.title: Changing the Rule
outline.summary: Introduce intervention as the act of changing the assignment rule ourselves — for example, deciding by a coin flip who gets tutoring — which cuts the link from PriorAchievement to TutoringAssignment and lets us see tutoring's own effect cleanly. Mention do(...) once as shorthand for 'changing the rule'.
outline.rag_focus: hard intervention replaces one assignment mechanism; intervention distribution can differ from observational distribution
outline.anchor_use: On the same three-variable graph, visually erase or cross out the arrow from PriorAchievement to TutoringAssignment to show what changes when we set the rule ourselves, then ask what the score difference would tell us now.
outline.target_misconception: Filtering to students who received tutoring is the same as assigning tutoring by design.
outline.interaction_hook: Ask visitors: 'If we flipped a coin to decide who gets tutoring, and tutored students still scored higher, what would that tell us that the school report could not?' Invite one or two responses before confirming the key insight.
outline.learning_arc_step: Ask the intervention question: what if we changed the rule?

anchor_case.scenario: A school report shows that students who attended tutoring sessions scored higher on the end-of-term test — but does tutoring itself deserve the credit?

PriorAchievement.description: What students knew before tutoring began.

TestScore.description: The later score we want to understand.

forbidden_edges: TestScore (Y) -> TutoringAssignment (T) in the same study window
simplifying_assumptions: Use one school-term snapshot: tutoring is assigned before the later test score is measured.
Later test scores could influence future tutoring, but that would need a time-indexed story.
anchor_case.rationale: The tutoring scenario uses a familiar school setting to make the gap between 'noticing a pattern' and 'proving a cause' immediately relatable to any public visitor.

anchor_plausibility_check.role_scope_match: The story is framed for public understanding rather than professional practice.
anchor_plausibility_check.magnitudes_reasonable: The scenario uses ordinary school-report comparisons and does not depend on numerical magnitudes.
anchor_plausibility_check.most_likely_expert_objection: Selection rules vary by school; the lesson treats prior achievement as one plausible hidden driver, not the only one.

domain_assumptions_used: Students can differ in prior achievement before tutoring starts.
Prior achievement can affect both tutoring assignment and later scores.

sections.content:
A school report lands on the principal's desk. Students who attended tutoring sessions scored noticeably higher on the end-of-term test. The headline practically writes itself: *Tutoring works!*

But wait — does it? Before we celebrate, let's look a little closer at where that score gap might actually be coming from.

[CONTEXT_IMAGE: A bright school noticeboard displaying a bar chart with two bars side by side. Left bar labelled 'No Tutoring', right bar labelled 'Tutoring', the right bar clearly taller. A cartoon magnifying glass hovers over the gap between the bars, with a question mark inside the lens. Warm classroom colours, friendly and inviting.]

> **After this mini lesson, you will be able to:**
> - Spot the difference between *noticing a pattern* and *proving a cause*.
> - Explain why students who get tutoring might already be different from those who don't.
> - Describe what it would take to truly test whether tutoring itself raises scores.

A cartoon magnifying glass hovers over the gap between the bars, with a question mark inside the lens. Warm classroom colours, friendly and inviting.]

sections.content:
Most of us share the same gut reaction when we see this report: *the tutoring caused the higher scores*. It feels obvious — tutored students did better, so tutoring must be the reason.

This instinct is understandable, but it has a blind spot. It assumes the two groups — tutored and not tutored — were identical in every way before tutoring started. In real schools, that is rarely true. Some students sign up for tutoring *because* they are already motivated or already doing well. Others are recommended for tutoring *because* a teacher spotted early promise. Either way, the groups were different from day one.

When we compare their final scores, we are not just measuring what tutoring added — we are also measuring everything those students brought with them before a single session began.

sections.section: Two Roads to a Higher Score
sections.content:
Think of it this way. Three things matter in this story:

- **Prior Achievement ($Z$)** — what a student already knew before tutoring started.
- **Tutoring Assignment ($T$)** — whether the student received tutoring.
- **Test Score ($Y$)** — the score we want to understand.

Here is the key insight: *Prior Achievement influences both of the other two variables.* Students with stronger prior achievement are more likely to be assigned to tutoring — and they are also more likely to score well on the test, tutoring or not.

So when we see tutored students scoring higher, there are two possible roads that score gap could have travelled:

1. **The tutoring road:** Tutoring → better test score. *(This is what we hope is true.)*
2. **The hidden road:** Strong prior achievement → selected for tutoring, AND strong prior achievement → higher test score anyway.

Both roads lead to the same destination — a score gap — but only the first one means tutoring deserves the credit. Just looking at the report, we cannot tell which road did the heavy lifting.

[CONTEXT_IMAGE: Two parallel roads drawn in a simple flat illustration style. Road 1 is labelled 'Tutoring Road' and shows a student icon walking through a tutoring session icon to reach a trophy icon for 'High Score'. Road 2 is labelled 'Hidden Road' and shows the same student icon already carrying a backpack labelled 'Strong Start', bypassing the tutoring session entirely and also reaching the same trophy. Both roads end at the same trophy, emphasising that the destination looks identical from the outside.]

sections.content:
Here is the causal map for our story. The arrows show which variable influences which.

```mermaid
graph LR
    Z[PriorAchievement] --> T[TutoringAssignment]
    Z[PriorAchievement] --> Y[TestScore]
    T[TutoringAssignment] --> Y[TestScore]
```

Notice that **PriorAchievement ($Z$)** has arrows pointing to *both* TutoringAssignment and TestScore. That makes it a hidden driver — it quietly shapes both sides of the comparison at the same time. When a variable does this, causal scientists call it a *confounder*.

The school report only showed us the arrow from T to Y. It did not — and could not — automatically separate that arrow from the two arrows flowing through Z.

**So what would actually settle the question?**

Imagine a different kind of study: instead of letting prior achievement decide who gets tutoring, we change the rule ourselves — we randomly assign students to tutoring regardless of how they were doing before. In causal language this is written as `do(TutoringAssignment)`, meaning we replace the old assignment rule with our own. When we do that, the arrow from PriorAchievement into TutoringAssignment disappears. The hidden road is closed. Any score gap we see now can only have come through the tutoring road.

[PEDAGOGICAL_IMAGE: Two side-by-side panels with a clean white background. Left panel titled 'What the report shows' displays three rounded rectangles labelled 'Prior Achievement (Z)', 'Tutoring (T)', and 'Test Score (Y)'. Bold orange arrows connect Z to T and Z to Y, and a blue arrow connects T to Y. A highlight box around Z reads 'Hidden driver flows here too'. Right panel titled 'If we randomly assign tutoring' shows the same three rectangles, but the orange arrow from Z to T is crossed out with a red X, leaving only the Z-to-Y orange arrow and the blue T-to-Y arrow intact. A label beneath the crossed arrow reads 'Rule changed — hidden road closed'. Both panels use the same colour coding so the difference is immediately obvious.]

sections.content:
**Question 1.** The school report shows tutored students scored higher. What is the *safest* conclusion to draw?

A. Tutoring definitely caused the higher scores.
B. There is a pattern, but prior achievement might explain part of the gap.
C. Prior achievement is the only reason for the gap.
D. The test was too easy for the tutored group.

---

**Question 2.** In the causal map, PriorAchievement has arrows pointing to both TutoringAssignment and TestScore. What does this make it?

A. A hidden driver that influences both sides of the comparison.
B. An outcome we are trying to explain.
C. A variable that tutoring controls.
D. An irrelevant background detail.

---

**Question 3.** A researcher randomly assigns students to tutoring, ignoring their prior achievement entirely. What does this change about the causal map?

A. It removes the arrow from TutoringAssignment to TestScore.
B. It removes the arrow from PriorAchievement to TestScore.
C. It removes the arrow from PriorAchievement to TutoringAssignment.
D. It adds a new arrow from TestScore back to TutoringAssignment.

---

<details>
<summary>Show Answers</summary>

**Answer 1: B.** The report shows a pattern, but because students with higher prior achievement were more likely to receive tutoring, the gap could partly reflect what they brought in — not only what tutoring added.

**Answer 2: A.** When one variable points to both the treatment and the outcome, it can secretly drive the comparison. That is exactly what a confounder does.

**Answer 3: C.** Random assignment means prior achievement no longer decides who gets tutoring, so the arrow from PriorAchievement into TutoringAssignment is replaced by the researcher's coin flip. The hidden road is closed.

</details>

> After this mini lesson, you will be able to:
> - Explain what it means to *change the assignment rule* for who gets tutoring
> - Describe how a coin-flip assignment cuts the link from PriorAchievement to TutoringAssignment
> - Say why the score difference we see *after* changing the rule is a cleaner measure of tutoring's own effect

Imagine a school that has always let high-achieving students sign up for tutoring first. When you look at the report later, tutored students scored higher — but were they already ahead to begin with? In the previous lesson we saw that PriorAchievement ($Z$) quietly shapes both who gets tutoring and how students score. That hidden link makes it hard to give tutoring the credit — or the blame.

This lesson is about one powerful move: instead of *observing* who ended up in tutoring, we *decide* who gets it ourselves, using something like a coin flip. That single change rewrites the story.

[CONTEXT_IMAGE: A split scene. On the left, a school hallway where students with gold stars on their folders walk toward a 'Tutoring Room' sign, suggesting self-selection by ability. On the right, a teacher flipping a large coin in front of a mixed group of students — some with gold stars, some without — all looking at the coin. A caption reads: 'Left: students choose. Right: the coin chooses.' Warm classroom lighting, simple flat-illustration style.]

sections.content:
**A common mix-up worth clearing up first.**

Many people think: *'If I just look only at the students who happened to get tutoring, I can see what tutoring does.'* It feels logical — you are focusing on the tutored group, after all.

But here is the catch: those students did not end up in tutoring by chance. PriorAchievement ($Z$) influenced who was assigned tutoring ($T$). So the tutored group is already a special group — likely stronger students to begin with. Filtering your view to that group does not remove the influence of prior achievement; it just hides it from sight.

Changing the rule is something different. It means we step in and *replace* how tutoring gets assigned — so prior achievement no longer has any say in who receives it.

In the original story, the assignment rule for TutoringAssignment ($T$) was something like: *'Students with higher prior achievement are more likely to get a spot.'* That rule is the arrow from Z to T in our graph.

When we change the rule — say, by flipping a coin for every student — we replace that rule entirely. The coin does not know anything about a student's prior achievement. So prior achievement no longer has any power over who gets tutoring. The arrow from Z to T is gone. This is what researchers call a **hard intervention**: one assignment mechanism is swapped out, and the old inputs to that mechanism lose their grip.

Shorthand for this idea: **do(TutoringAssignment := coin flip)** — the `do(...)` is just a compact way of saying *'we changed the rule ourselves.'*

Now compare two groups: students whose coin landed on tutoring, and students whose coin landed on no tutoring. Because the coin ignored prior achievement, both groups are, on average, equally mixed in ability. Any difference in TestScore ($Y$) between the two groups can no longer be blamed on prior achievement sneaking in. What remains is tutoring's own effect — clean and direct.

Here is the original causal graph, with all three arrows in place:

```mermaid
graph LR
    Z[PriorAchievement Z] --> T[TutoringAssignment T]
    Z --> Y[TestScore Y]
    T --> Y
```

**Question 1.** When we assign tutoring by coin flip, what happens to the arrow from PriorAchievement ($Z$) to TutoringAssignment ($T$)?

A. It gets stronger because more students are involved.
B. It is cut — prior achievement no longer determines who gets tutoring.
C. It reverses direction, so tutoring now affects prior achievement.
D. Nothing changes; the arrow stays exactly as it was.

---

**Question 2.** After the coin-flip assignment, we compare the average TestScore ($Y$) of tutored students with the average TestScore of non-tutored students. What does a difference in scores most likely reflect now?

A. The effect of tutoring itself, because prior achievement is no longer steering who got it.
B. The fact that high-achieving students still signed up for tutoring on their own.
C. A mistake in the coin flip, because scores should always be equal.
D. The direct effect of prior achievement on test scores.

---

**Question 3.** A friend says: 'I can get the same clean answer by just looking only at the low-achieving students who happened to attend tutoring.' What is the problem with this plan?

A. There are not enough low-achieving students to study.
B. Low-achieving students never attend tutoring.
C. Filtering to students who happened to attend tutoring still reflects the original assignment rule — prior achievement still influenced who ended up there.
D. It would work perfectly; filtering and coin-flip assignment give identical results.

---

<details>
<summary>Show Answers</summary>

**Answer 1: B.** Changing the rule to a coin flip replaces the old mechanism entirely. Prior achievement no longer has any path into TutoringAssignment, so that arrow is cut.

**Answer 2: A.** Because the coin ignored prior achievement, both groups are comparably mixed in ability on average. A score difference between them points to tutoring as the cause, not a pre-existing ability gap.

**Answer 3: C.** Filtering to students who *happened* to attend tutoring does not remove the original rule — those students were still selected partly because of their prior achievement. Only replacing the rule itself (for example, with a coin flip) breaks that link.

</details>
